name: Justinian I
info: Justinian I, called Justinian the Great, was Roman emperor at Constantinople from 527 to 565, remembered for reconquering North Africa and Italy, codifying Roman law in the Corpus Juris Civilis and rebuilding the Hagia Sophia.

facts.born: Around 482, according to Procopius in the hamlet of Tauresium in Dardania; of a peasant family thought to be of Thraco-Roman or Illyro-Roman origin, nephew of the future emperor Justin I
facts.died: 14 November 565, in his sleep at Constantinople, childless; buried in the Church of the Holy Apostles
facts.role: Consul and commander of the army of the east from 520; nobilissimus and caesar from 525; co-emperor from 1 April 527; sole Roman emperor from 1 August 527 to 565
facts.known: the Corpus Juris Civilis; the reconquest of North Africa, Italy and southern Hispania; the Hagia Sophia; the Nika riots; wars with the Sasanian Empire; enforcing Chalcedonian orthodoxy; the Plague of Justinian

t: Brought to Constantinople and educated by his uncle Justin, Justinian was the power behind the throne in Justin's last years and ruled alone from 527 to 565.
His generals Belisarius and Narses won back North Africa and Italy and his forces took southern Hispania, but the long Gothic war devastated Italy and only Africa and Sicily proved lasting gains.

His codification of Roman law became the basis of civil law in many states, while his laws against pagans, Jews, Samaritans, heretics and homosexual men show the harsh side of his drive for unity of faith.
dyk: In the early 550s two monks smuggled silkworm eggs from Central Asia to Constantinople, and silk became a product of the empire itself.
ev: Justinian is crowned co-emperor on 1 April and becomes sole ruler after Justin I dies on 1 August
The first draft of the Codex Justinianeus is issued; the Neoplatonic Academy in Athens is closed
The Nika riots nearly overthrow him and end in a massacre in the Hippodrome; the Eternal Peace is made with Persia
Belisarius defeats the Vandals at Ad Decimum and Tricamarum and takes Carthage
The rebuilt Hagia Sophia is completed
Belisarius enters Ravenna, while Khosrau I breaks the Eternal Peace and sacks Antioch
Narses defeats the Ostrogoths at Busta Gallorum, where Totila is killed; Spania is founded in southern Hispania
Justinian dies and is succeeded by his nephew Justin II

sections.early:
According to his contemporary Procopius, Justinian was born in the hamlet of Tauresium in the province of Dardania, near the fortress of Bederiana; later scholarship places his birth around 482. Tauresium is most commonly identified with Gradište near the village of Taor, southeast of Skopje in present-day North Macedonia, though its distance from Justiniana Prima, the city he later founded nearby, has kept the location under debate. He came from a peasant family thought to be of Thraco-Roman or Illyro-Roman origin and was a native speaker of Latin, among the last Eastern Roman emperors to be one.

His mother, Vigilantia, was the sister of Justin, commander of one of the imperial guard units, the Excubitors. Justin adopted him, brought him to Constantinople and had him educated in jurisprudence, theology and Roman history; the name Iustinianus reflects that adoption. Justinian served as a candidatus, one of 40 men chosen from the palace guards as the emperor's bodyguard. John Malalas described him as short, fair-skinned, curly-haired, round-faced and handsome; Procopius, in similar terms, compared him to the emperor Domitian, perhaps an allusion to one of the most despised men in Roman history.
sections.rise:
When the emperor Anastasius died in 518, Justin was proclaimed emperor with considerable help from Justinian. Several sources claim that Justinian acted as virtual regent long before he was made associate emperor, though there is no conclusive evidence of this; as Justin became senile, Justinian became the ruler in fact. After the assassination of the general Vitalian in 520, orchestrated by Justinian or Justin, he was made consul and commander of the army of the east. In the church he helped end the Acacian schism with Rome soon after 518. In 525 he received the titles of nobilissimus and caesar, marking him as heir.

Around 525 he married his mistress Theodora, an actress and prostitute some twenty years his junior; the marriage, made possible because Justin had lifted restrictions on marriages with ex-actresses, caused a scandal, but Theodora became very influential in politics. Justinian was crowned co-emperor on 1 April 527 and became sole ruler on Justin's death on 1 August 527. He was known as "the emperor who never sleeps". Around him were able men: Tribonian, his legal adviser; Peter the Patrician; the finance ministers John the Cappadocian and Peter Barsymes, who collected taxes more efficiently than any before them; and the generals Belisarius and Narses.
sections.deeds:
Justinian had Tribonian revise the whole of Roman law, something never attempted before. The Codex Justinianeus appeared in draft on 7 April 529 and in final form in 534, the Digest in 533, then the Institutiones, a textbook, and the Novellae, new laws issued in Greek. Together they are known as the Corpus Juris Civilis. His laws protected prostitutes and women forced into prostitution, returned dowries to widows, gave slaves the right to plead for their freedom and made killing a slave murder, and showed concern for abandoned and illegitimate children.

Having made the Eternal Peace with Persia in 532 for 11,000 pounds of gold, he turned west. In 533 Belisarius sailed with about 15,000 men, defeated the Vandals and took Carthage. From 535 Belisarius took Sicily, Naples and Rome and in 540 entered Ravenna; after Totila's revival of the Ostrogoths, Narses with about 35,000 men won at Busta Gallorum and Mons Lactarius in 552 and defeated a Frankish invasion at Casilinum in 554. A force of 2,000 men took Cartagena and founded the province of Spania. The empire reached its territorial zenith in 555. At home he rebuilt the Hagia Sophia, completed in 537 under Isidore of Miletus and Anthemius of Tralles, the Church of the Holy Apostles and Saints Sergius and Bacchus, and built fortifications, the Basilica Cistern, the Sangarius Bridge and Justiniana Prima.
sections.opponents:
His rule was not universally popular. In January 532 the chariot-racing factions united in the Nika riots, forced the dismissal of Tribonian and two other ministers and tried to crown the senator Hypatius. Justinian considered flight but stayed, apparently at Theodora's urging; Belisarius and Mundus suppressed the revolt, and Procopius relates that 30,000 unarmed civilians were killed in the Hippodrome. A conspiracy against his life was discovered as late as 562. Procopius, who praised his buildings, wrote in the Secret History a hostile portrait of a cruel, corrupt and incompetent ruler. The heavy taxes laid on Italy were deeply resented, and some historians argue he dangerously stretched the empire's resources.

His drive for unity of faith under the Chalcedonian church brought persecution. Laws barred philosophers, astrologers, heretics, pagans, Manicheans, Jews and Samaritans from public office, destroyed their places of worship and restricted their property; pagan practice was restricted even in private, and the Samaritans, who repeatedly revolted, were forbidden to make wills in 529. Laws against male homosexual acts were applied retrospectively on a single witness, and those convicted were mutilated and paraded. His attempts to win over the Miaphysites satisfied none of the parties; the condemnation of the Three Chapters, to which Pope Vigilius was forced to assent at Constantinople, caused a schism in the west.
sections.last:
The later reign was burdened by disaster. In 540 Khosrau I broke the Eternal Peace, sacked Antioch and forced Justinian to pay 5,000 pounds of gold and 500 more a year; the war ended with a fifty years' peace in 562 that required an annual Roman tribute for Lazica. The plague that struck in 541-543 afflicted the emperor himself, who recovered; it was traditionally believed to have killed tens of millions, though recent research argues the sources overstated it and scholars remain divided. Theodora died in 548, possibly of cancer. In 559 Kutrigurs and Sklavinoi under Zabergan threatened Constantinople and were repulsed by the aged Belisarius.

In his last years Justinian grew isolated and relied on a small circle of advisers. He became increasingly fixated on religion and intolerant, yet less ruthless: after an earthquake in 557 he gave up wearing his crown and gave to the poor, and in the 560s he showed clemency to conspirators against him and pardoned Belisarius, accused of joining the plot. He died in his sleep on the night of 14 November 565, childless. His nephew Justin II, married to Theodora's niece Sophia, was quickly acclaimed emperor, and Justinian was buried in a golden tomb in the Church of the Holy Apostles, which was robbed when the Fourth Crusade pillaged the city in 1204.
sections.legacy:
The Corpus Juris Civilis ensured the survival of Roman law. It underlay later Byzantine law in the Basilika, passed from Italy to Western Europe in the 12th century to become the basis of much Continental law, spread with European empires to the Americas and reached Eastern Europe and Russia; it is still the basis of civil law in many modern states. The Hagia Sophia remained the centre of eastern Christianity for centuries. Of his conquests only Africa and Sicily proved lasting, and much of Italy was lost soon after his death, though Rome, Naples and Ravenna were kept. Some historians hold that Africa and southern Italy paid for themselves; Peter Sarris argues the plague made the reconquest harder and costlier.

Justinian is widely regarded as a saint by Eastern Christians and is commemorated with Theodora on 14 November. In Dante's Paradiso he appears as a spirit in the sphere of Mercury, a lawgiver and restorer of Rome who confesses that fame as well as duty moved him. Historians draw on Procopius, whose Wars and Buildings are more favourable than his Secret History, and on the more neutral chronicle of John Malalas. Novelists from Robert Graves in Count Belisarius to Guy Gavriel Kay have portrayed him, often as jealous of his greatest general.

summary: Justinian I ruled the Eastern Roman Empire from 527 to 565. His generals won back North Africa, Italy and southern Hispania at great cost, his jurists compiled the Corpus Juris Civilis, and he rebuilt the Hagia Sophia, while the Nika riots, persecution of religious minorities, war with Persia and plague marked his reign.

notes: Birth year 482 is 'later scholarship'; circa set true.
Procopius's claim of 5,000,000 dead in the African war is left out of the text: J. A. S. Evans casts doubt on it, and there was no room to give both.
The article's line about Manicheans burned 'around 450' predates Justinian's reign and was left out.
The founding of Spania is dated to the 552 expedition in the article; placed in the 552 event.
